experiment: X6 backlog drain capacity across instances (career sprint W7)
upstream: simulated upstream (scripts/stub-upstream.sh), fixed chat latency 700-900 ms; not a real provider, zero API cost

setup.basis: stub upstream, separate executor JVMs sharing one run database; all tasks created on instance a through ResearchRunService.create()
setup.runDir: local-data/agentic-research/runs/career_X6_v1 (x6-report.md, x6-summary.json, per-cell instance logs and result.json)
setup.note: each cell gets a fresh isolated run database and a fresh stub upstream; a small fixed corpus is imported once before the matrix

definitions.drain: from the submission of the 300 tasks to the last terminal event, database clock
definitions.queueWait: task creation to its first claim; percentiles are nearest-rank
definitions.serviceTime: first RUN_STARTED to the terminal event
definitions.slotBoundPerMin: instances x slots / mean service time, the ceiling if claiming were free and instantaneous
definitions.claimCalls: application-side timing of the claim statement (pooled connection + transaction + statements); one call may claim several tasks, up to the free slots
definitions.invariants: started exactly once by one executor, no takeover or release, exactly one terminal event, at most one ARTIFACT, contiguous event sequence, status COMPLETED

loadBalance.note: on 3 instances 286-288 of 300 tasks were claimed by polling; the rest went straight into the submitting instance's free slots

conclusion: Throughput scales linearly with instances: 12.2 / 24.0 / 35.8 tasks per minute at poll 5 s (speedup 1.00 / 1.98 / 2.95), 13.3 / 26.5 / 39.7 at poll 1 s (1.00 / 1.99 / 2.98). Repetitions agree within 0.2%.

The bottleneck is the slots, not the database. Every cell lands at 85-95% of the slot bound (instances x slots / service time); the remaining gap is the poll interval, which idles a freed slot for up to one interval. Dropping the poll from 5 s to 1 s recovers most of it: +9.5% / +10.1% / +10.7% throughput.

The claim statement is not a cost: 4.1-5.6 ms mean, 85 ms worst case, 52-231 calls per instance per 300-task drain (one call takes several tasks at once). Claim time is under 0.12% of the drain on any instance. Idle polling is exactly one claim query per interval per instance (0.2/s at poll 5 s, 1.0/s at poll 1 s).
A backlog never fails at the door: 0 of 3600 tasks rejected at submit; tasks that found no free slot waited in the database and were picked up by polling.

At least once did not become more than once under load: 0 invariant failures over 3600 runs (every run started exactly once, one terminal event, at most one artifact, contiguous event sequence, all COMPLETED).
Queue wait is what a backlog costs: with 300 tasks and 3 instances, P50 242 s and P95 470 s at poll 5 s. Wait scales down with instances (1x / 0.51x / 0.34x).
limits: Simulated upstream with a fixed 700-900 ms chat latency: this measures the queue and the executors, not a provider. Against a real provider the ceiling is the vendor's rate limit.
One host, one PostgreSQL: instances are separate JVMs on the same machine sharing one database, so this does not cover network latency, a connection-pool ceiling, or a loaded database.
Only up to 3 instances and 2 slots each; linearity beyond that is not measured. The database claim has headroom at 0.34 claim calls/s, but no saturation point was found.
pg_stat_statements is not enabled in the image, so claim cost is timed application-side and includes the pooled connection and transaction.
Single-agent mode, no fault injection: X6 measures clean drains. Failure behaviour is X2 and X3.
